q: What is LastSeen?
a: A search system that brings what witnesses say into search planning. Muse Spark turns each report into weighted, checked scenarios on the map, the drone re-plans and flies the search itself, and SAM 3.1 and Muse Spark check every photo for a person who may be only a few dozen pixels wide. One volunteer launches it, swaps batteries and stays in command.

q: What is new about it? How is it different?
a: Search planning already uses probability: published statistics on how far people go, and search managers who weigh scenarios by hand. The standard search pattern ignores witnesses altogether. What is new: LastSeen reads every report as it comes in, turns it into weighted scenarios with weight kept on 'the witness is wrong', and the drone re-plans from them in seconds. The model decides what the words mean; code decides the numbers and checks every place it names.

q: Who is it for?
a: Volunteer search teams, often one person with one drone, searching for someone who has walked away, such as an older person with dementia. These are searches where every minute matters and nobody can watch hundreds of photos closely.

q: Is this a real search? Is Margaret real?
a: No. Margaret is fictional and the searches are simulated. The valley (Saint-Ursanne, Switzerland), its maps and aerial imagery are real, and every photo decision uses real drone photos of real people from the HERIDAL dataset.

q: How does the simulated search work?
a: A hidden person walks over the real map's terrain and paths, following behaviour rules. The planners never see where she is: they only get the witness reports and what their own photos show. Each photo of her is judged by a recorded SAM 3.1 and Muse Spark answer on a real drone photo of a person her size.

q: What is the expanding square?
a: The standard pattern search teams fly: square loops that grow outward from where the person was last seen. It is hard to beat; in our tests, smarter map-based planners didn't. Its weakness is that it can't react to a witness.

q: What does the team planner do differently?
a: It flies the expanding square until a witness reports a sighting. Then the drone breaks off to search where Muse Spark's reading of that report points, while the probability map keeps updating. With several drones, one breaks off and the others keep flying the square.

q: What do the colours on the race maps mean?
a: The yellow dot is the drone. The orange-yellow glow is where the planner thinks she is. Blue is ground the drone has photographed. A green ring marks the find, and the red line is her real path, shown only when you reveal it.

q: What does Muse Spark do?
a: Three jobs. It reads the brief and every witness report into weighted explanations of where she might be, using named places on the real map. It grades each witness. And it checks each possible person SAM 3.1 finds, on a close-up, before a reviewer sees it.

q: What does SAM 3.1 do?
a: It looks at each drone photo, in 1000-pixel tiles, and proposes everything that might be a person, with a confidence. Muse Spark then checks each proposal, so the reviewer only sees the alarms.

q: What does Muse Voice Transcribe do?
a: It turns a spoken brief into text, so a volunteer can say what the family told them instead of typing it.

q: Where does the map of likely places come from?
a: Before anyone says anything, from published statistics on how far people of this kind usually go. Then Muse Spark's reading of the brief and reports is blended in, with a share always kept on 'none of these', because witnesses are often wrong.

q: How do you stop the model from making things up?
a: Code checks every answer. Each explanation must quote words that really appear in the reports or on the map, or it is thrown out. Numbers are clamped to sensible ranges. Witness grades must quote the brief. And this help box can only show answers we wrote.

q: How does Muse Spark turn words into a map?
a: It reads the brief and every report and proposes up to 5 competing explanations of where she is, each made of simple shapes measured from the house: a direction, a distance band, near a path, water or woods, or a spot where someone was seen. Code turns each shape into a map layer on top of the distance statistics and weights it by Spark's probability, always keeping at least 15% on 'none of these'.

q: What if witnesses disagree?
a: Each story becomes its own weighted explanation, so the map keeps both until the drone's photos rule areas out. No report gets all the weight: at least 15% always stays on none of them.

q: Why not let the AI plan the route itself?
a: The model decides what the reports mean; code decides the numbers. Routes, battery limits and the probability updates are ordinary code that can be tested and replayed exactly, and the drone never waits on a model.

q: What happens if the model is down or gives a bad answer?
a: The search carries on with the statistics alone and the failure is shown on the page; the drone never waits. Explanations that fail the checks, such as a quote that isn't in the reports, are dropped, and numbers are clamped to sensible ranges.

q: What if a witness is wrong?
a: The map keeps weight on other explanations, and the square's ground still gets covered. In the race with a wrong sighting, the detour cost 28 minutes. Across all wrong sightings in our development scenarios, the team planner did as well as the square.

q: What are the witness grades?
a: For each person in the brief, Muse Spark says who they are, whether they know her, whether they saw it themselves, and whether anyone else backs it up, and grades them strong, fair or weak. The grades are shown to help a person judge; they don't change the map.

q: How much better is it than the standard pattern?
a: On 200 development scenarios with one drone, 53% were found within 2 hours, against 46% with the expanding square alone, and half were found by 1 h 38 instead of 2 h 58. The final result comes from 200 different scenarios fixed in advance and run once.

q: Couldn't a volunteer just fly to where the witness said?
a: Yes, and on our simulated reports that gets most of the gain: restarting the square on the spot the witness named found 51% within 2 hours, against 46% for the square and 53% for LastSeen (development scenarios; LastSeen's edge over the volunteer, +2 points, is within the noise). The simulator's reports are simple sentences anyone can read exactly. Muse Spark is for what real witnesses say: named places, vague directions, several reports that disagree, read in seconds while the drone flies, with weight kept on the witness being wrong.

q: Is the race you show cherry-picked?
a: It is one of the 200 development scenarios, chosen because it is in a real valley. The page also shows a race where the sighting was wrong and the square wins. The overall numbers come from all scenarios, not from the races shown.

q: Did you tune it on the test?
a: No. We only tuned on development scenarios. The final 200 scenarios, the measure and the wording of the result were written down before they were ever run, and they run once after the feature freeze, whatever they show.

q: How well does it spot people in photos?
a: Measured on real drone photos of 227 people: 79% of people about 44 pixels wide, which is a person seen from about 100 m, were found in a single photo. In a 4-hour one-drone search, a reviewer checks about 150 close-ups instead of 660 photos.

q: How much reviewing time does the photo check save?
a: A 4-hour one-drone search takes about 660 full photos. Croatian mountain rescuers report 5 to 45 seconds to look through one (Gotovac et al., 2020), so that is about 1 to 8 hours of looking, falling further behind as the drone keeps flying. SAM 3.1 and Muse Spark leave about 150 close-ups, each one spot to accept or reject. It finds 79% of people that size in a single photo, so it saves the hours of looking; it doesn't replace the reviewer's judgement on each alarm.

q: How many false alarms does the reviewer see?
a: About 150 close-ups in a 4-hour one-drone search, nearly all of them not her. That is about one every 2 minutes while the drone flies, each one spot to accept or reject.

q: Does it work at night or with a thermal camera?
a: Not tested. Detection was measured on daytime colour photos; a thermal camera would need its own measurement.

q: What about wind, rain or fog?
a: Not modelled. The simulator flies in calm, clear conditions; bad weather would shorten flights and lower detection, and we haven't measured by how much.

q: Why fly at 100 m?
a: In the simulator, 100-120 m found more people within 2 hours than 40-80 m: each photo covers more ground and a person is still about 44 pixels wide. 100 m also leaves a margin under the usual 120 m legal limit.

q: Can it see people under trees?
a: Less well. The test photos have nobody under trees, so the simulator assumes the drone sees a person in forest at 40% of the open-ground rate. In the Saint-Ursanne race she is under trees, and it took four passes over her before a photo found her.

q: Is the find photo really her?
a: No. It is a real drone photo of a real person her size from the HERIDAL dataset, used as a stand-in. The simulator decides each find on photos like it.

q: Does the AI fly the drone? Who flies it?
a: Its autopilot does. LastSeen plans each battery's search and re-plans when a report comes in; the drone flies it at a set height, sends its photos to be checked, and comes home when the battery runs low. The volunteer launches it, swaps the battery and stays in command. In the simulator this runs end to end; LastSeen isn't connected to a real drone yet (see 'Does it work with a real drone?').

q: How does a new route reach the drone mid-flight?
a: Over the radio link every drone keeps with its controller at the base. It carries flight data down and commands up, so when a witness calls in, LastSeen sends the new route while the drone is still in the air. Photos need more bandwidth (see 'How do the photos get checked during the flight?').

q: Is it fully autonomous? Why does it need a volunteer or a person at all?
a: Flying and deciding where to go are automatic. A person stays for four things: the law (in the EU's open category the remote pilot must be able to take control at any time, and flying beyond sight needs a permit), swapping batteries (a drone dock could do that), checking the alarm close-ups before anyone is sent out, and passing on what witnesses phone in.

q: How do the photos get checked during the flight?
a: The drone sends each photo back as it is taken, and SAM 3.1 and Muse Spark check it straight away: one photo of about 5 MB every 10 seconds, around 4 Mbit/s. Some enterprise drones can send photos during flight; on others a small onboard computer with a 4G modem can. If photos only come off after landing, they are checked at the battery swap and a find waits up to 25 minutes. The simulator checks each photo as it is taken.

q: Why not just watch the drone's live video?
a: In the drone's full photos a person seen from 100 m is about 44 pixels wide; in a 720p live feed on a phone she is about 14, and the pilot is also watching the sky and the battery. SAM 3.1 and Muse Spark check every full photo, so a person only looks at the alarms.

q: Does it work with a real drone?
a: Not connected yet. Each battery's mission exports for QGroundControl, which works with most MAVLink drones, and loads correctly; it hasn't been flown. The next step is sending missions and route changes over the drone's radio link, and receiving its photos in flight.

q: What happens when the drone finds someone?
a: Muse Spark writes a short handover for the ground team from facts code works out: where she is in coordinates, distance and direction from where she was last seen, the ground there, the nearest path, and what the photo shows. Code checks that every number in it comes from those facts.

q: Does it need the Meta API, or can it run on open weights?
a: Every Muse Spark job can run on Muse Spark Open, Meta's open-weight model, served by Baseten. On the same 200 scenarios it found 52% within 2 hours against 53% with Muse Spark, and it found 177 people in the test photos against 179. On this page, 'Use open weights' reads a brief with it.

q: What does it cost to run?
a: At today's prices, checking one drone photo (12 tiles) costs about four cents, so the 660 photos of a 4-hour one-drone search cost about $25. Reading a brief costs about one cent, and reading every report in a search costs under a cent more.

q: What about more than one drone?
a: LastSeen plans every drone's route at once: when a witness calls, one breaks off to follow the report while the others keep the square, which is hard to coordinate by hand under pressure. With three drones it found 66% within 2 hours against the square's 64% on development scenarios (+2 points, 95% interval +0.5 to +4), and it keeps going if one drone fails. Three drones cover the square fast enough that the order matters less, so the gain is largest with one drone. Each drone still needs a pilot able to take control, so three drones mean a small team.

q: Does it only work for people with dementia? What about hikers?
a: The results here are for dementia searches, the case it was built for. The simulator can also make the person walk like a hiker, as a stress test, but hiker searches haven't been evaluated.

q: What if a drone fails?
a: With several drones, the others take over its unfinished part of the search. The evaluation includes one of three drones failing at a random time between 15 minutes and 2 hours in.

q: What was built during the hackathon?
a: Everything here was built between 27 October and 4 November 2026: the simulator, the planners, the model checks, the detection measurements, this page and the hosted demo.

q: Did search-and-rescue experts check this?
a: We wrote to researchers and rescue organisations, and three researchers replied with their views on witnesses, statistics and maps that change mid-search. That is not an endorsement of LastSeen.

q: Are uploaded photos stored?
a: No. A photo you check is sent to the models, checked and discarded.

q: What is needed before real use?
a: Connecting to a real drone (missions and route changes over its radio link, photos back in flight), a test flight over open ground, and a trial with a volunteer search team on a training exercise. The simulator's limits are listed in docs/evaluation.md in the repository.

q: Can I use it on a real search today?
a: No. It is a tested prototype: not yet connected to a real drone, and not yet tried by a search team. It shows how the search would work, not a tool to rely on.

q: How does this question box work?
a: If your question shares most of its words with a written question, that answer appears at once, with no model call. Otherwise Muse Spark Open picks which written answers fit, or none if the question is off topic. It can only return answer ids, so you only ever see answers we wrote.

q: Can someone run up your bill through this box?
a: Written answers are free. A question that needs Muse Spark Open costs about a tenth of a cent, each visitor gets at most 10 model requests an hour, and the hosted demo stops all paid calls at a fixed spending cap.

q: Can I reuse the code? Is it open source?
a: Yes, under the MIT licence. The drone photos are from HERIDAL (CC BY 3.0), the aerial imagery is © swisstopo and the map data © OpenStreetMap contributors.

q: Where is the code?
a: In the public repository linked at the top of the page, with the evaluation plan, the parameter sources and the commands to reproduce every number.
